fields.title: Polka: the platform requested by the wrong people
fields.summary: A strategic session proposed opening a public API. Recommendation due in two weeks.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do you recommend? State the cost of your decision.
fields.brief/role: You are the Polka product manager.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a buyer app, and a partner portal.
fields.brief/context: You are the Polka product manager. A strategic session brought up opening a public API to "become a platform like our competitors did." You need to provide a recommendation in two weeks.
fields.brief/objective: Respond to the platform proposal based on actual demand rather than buzzwords.
fields.brief/constraints: Two weeks for the recommendation. Opening the API takes six weeks and half a headcount for ongoing support.
fields.brief/task: Provide a recommendation and justify what you are not doing.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A public API is a commitment, not a storefront
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Opening a contract to the outside world is easy, but closing it is nearly impossible: you must maintain compatibility for consumers you do not know, and every change slows down. Therefore, decide based on named demand. If demand comes from partners, it is cheaper to serve them via the partner circuit; if there is no demand at all, it is more honest to collect requests and return in a quarter with numbers.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Two inventory system integrators want to build modules for retail chains. One startup wants to build a price comparison service on top of our search results. Zero requests from buyers.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: 900 contracted partners, self-service launched, chain onboarding time is 4 days. 140 support tickets per quarter, reduced to 40 after documentation rework.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: Opened a public API a year ago. Their catalog has 11 apps, of which 3 have been updated in the last six months.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: Opening an API takes 6 weeks for key management, sandbox, and catalog. Support is estimated at half a headcount ongoing.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Open a public API. 6 weeks plus ongoing support.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: meets session expectations. Judging by the competitor, an ecosystem will not appear on its own. Creates obligations to unknown consumers and slows down changes. Requires resolving partner consent for price publication.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Do not open, enhance partner self-service and modules
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: 3 weeks. Finish the sandbox and documentation, help two integrators build modules for inventory systems.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: covers real demand—it comes from chain integrators, not the market. Does not create obligations to unknowns. Does not fulfill the "become a platform" wording, and you will have to explain this.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Open a limited public API for catalog read-only access
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Open a limited public API for catalog read-only access. 4 weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: a compromise that serves exactly the price comparison startup—meaning a consumer whose product works against us. Requires partner consent. The least useful option given the noticeable cost.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Delay decision, collect demand over the quarter
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Zero weeks. Access request form, request counter.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: cheap and honest. In a quarter, you will have a factual picture of demand. Looks like dodging a decision unless accompanied by analysis.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not verify the reasons for opening the API
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Does not read the questionnaire and legal constraints as part of the solution
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Does not evaluate public contract backward compatibility as an obligation
